question: What separates the engine compartment in each nacelle from the rest of the airframe structure?

options.text: A firewall, with fire-resistant matting covered on the engine side by stainless steel cladding
A simple aluminum bulkhead with no fire protection
A CFRP bulkhead identical to the main spar material
A firewall made of the same GFRP/CFRP sandwich as the wing skins

explanation: AFM 7.2 describes a firewall per nacelle with fire-resistant matting, covered on the engine side by stainless steel cladding.

question: What are the two main spars of the airframe, and what are they part of?

options.text: Steel items that are part of the landing gear structure
CFRP items that are part of the center wing
Aluminum items that are part of the fuselage nose
GFRP items that are part of the empennage

explanation: AFM 7.2: the two main spars are CFRP items, and both they and the two nacelles are part of the center wing, which is bolted to the fuselage.

question: What is installed in each wing as part of the fuel system?

options.text: A steel fuel tank
A fiberglass fuel tank
An aluminum fuel tank
A composite bladder-type fuel cell

explanation: AFM 7.2 states an aluminum fuel tank is installed in each of the wings.

question: What type of tail does the DA 42 NG have?

options.text: A conventional low-mounted tail of aluminum construction
A cruciform tail of CFRP construction
A V-tail (butterfly) configuration
A 'T' tail of GFRP/CFRP semi-monocoque construction

explanation: AFM 7.2 describes a 'T' tail of GFRP/CFRP semi-monocoque construction, with twin-spar stabilizers.

question: What type of landing gear does the DA 42 NG have?

options.text: A fully retractable, hydraulically operated, tricycle landing gear
A fixed tricycle landing gear
A fully retractable, pneumatically operated, tailwheel gear
A partially retractable tricycle gear with a fixed nose wheel

explanation: AFM 7.5: the landing gear is a fully retractable, hydraulically operated tricycle gear, unlike the DA40's fixed gear.

question: How long does landing gear extension normally take?

options.text: 30-40 seconds
6-10 seconds
1-2 seconds
20 seconds

explanation: AFM 7.5 states gear extension normally takes 6-10 seconds; manual extension in an emergency may take up to 20 seconds.

question: What keeps the landing gear in the retracted position in flight?

options.text: Aerodynamic loads holding the gear doors closed
Spring tension alone, identical to the extension mechanism
Hydraulic pressure on the actuators, backed by a pressurized gas accumulator
Mechanical uplock hooks alone, with no hydraulic assistance

explanation: AFM 7.5: hydraulic pressure keeps the gear retracted, with a pressurized gas accumulator replacing pressure lost to normal actuator leakage, avoiding continuous pump cycling.

question: What assists the hydraulic system in extending and locking the landing gear down?

options.text: A secondary electric motor per gear leg
Bungee cords attached to each gear door
Nothing; extension is purely hydraulic with no mechanical assist
Springs, which also maintain force on the downlock hooks

explanation: AFM 7.5: springs assist gear extension and locking, maintaining force on each downlock hook until released by hydraulic pressure.

question: Below what power-lever setting does the gear warning horn sound if the landing gear is retracted?

options.text: Approximately 20%
Approximately 50%
Approximately 10%
Approximately 30%

explanation: AFM 7.5: if a power lever is below approximately 20% while the gear is retracted, the warning horn sounds and a CHECK GEAR caution appears.

question: After take-off, before what airspeed should the landing gear be retracted?

options.text: 165 KIAS
152 KIAS
188 KIAS
135 KIAS

explanation: AFM 7.5: the gear should be retracted before 152 KIAS is exceeded (matching vLOR); it may be extended at any speed up to 188 KIAS.

question: What prevents the landing gear from retracting inadvertently while the airplane is on the ground?

options.text: A mechanical ground lock pin that must be removed manually
The ELECT. MASTER switch position alone
An electric squat switch
The parking brake interlock

explanation: AFM 7.5: an electric squat switch prevents the hydraulic valve from switching to retract while the airplane is on the ground and the master switch is on.

question: How is the emergency (manual) landing gear extended in the event of a hydraulic failure?

options.text: By a dedicated hand-crank located in the baggage compartment
By switching ELECT. MASTER OFF and then back ON three times
By an electric backup pump activated from the co-pilot's side panel
By pulling the emergency gear extension lever, which relieves hydraulic pressure and lets the gear fall free by gravity

explanation: AFM 7.5: pulling the emergency gear extension lever relieves hydraulic pressure so gravity extends and locks the gear; the gear selector should first be placed DOWN.

question: How is the nose gear steered?

options.text: By full rudder pedal travel, assisted by a damping element that prevents shimmy
By a separate hand-operated tiller on the center console
By differential braking only, with no direct steering linkage
By the elevator trim wheel, which is mechanically linked to the nose gear

explanation: AFM 7.5: the nose gear is steerable via full rudder pedal travel, with a damping element preventing shimmy; the steering linkage disengages once the gear retracts.

question: What type of brakes are fitted to the main landing gear?

options.text: Pneumatically operated disk brakes
Hydraulically operated disk brakes, individually operated by toe pedals
Mechanically operated drum brakes, operated by a hand lever
Electrically actuated disk brakes with no manual backup

explanation: AFM 7.5 describes hydraulically operated disk brakes on the main gear wheels, individually toe-pedal operated.

question: Which engine's heat is used for the front seats and cabin floor heating, and which for canopy defrost?

options.text: Both functions use LH engine heat exclusively
Both functions use RH engine heat exclusively
RH engine heat for seats/floor; LH engine heat for canopy defrost
LH engine heat for seats/floor; RH engine heat for canopy defrost

explanation: AFM 7.8: the RH engine's heat serves the front seats and floor, while the LH engine's heat is used to defrost the canopy.

question: What is the maximum airspeed permitted before take-off with the front canopy in the 'cooling gap' position?

options.text: 117 KIAS, matching the emergency-opening limit
140 KIAS
There is no restriction; the cooling gap may remain open for the whole flight
This is only for ground operation — the canopy must be fully closed and locked before take-off

explanation: AFM 7.8 warns the front canopy may be in the cooling-gap position on the ground only; it must be completely closed and locked before take-off.

question: If OÄM 42-205 is installed, what emergency tool is stowed under the co-pilot's seat for breaking through the canopy?

options.text: An emergency axe
A fire extinguisher
A crash axe stored in the tail cone
An emergency egress hammer, standard on every DA 42 NG

explanation: AFM 7.8: with OÄM 42-205 installed, an emergency axe is stowed under the co-pilot's seat; OÄM 42-304 instead installs an emergency egress hammer in the same location.
